name: Dualism
statement: The mind and the physical are, in some fundamental way, two distinct and irreducible kinds of thing.
statementAccent: two distinct and irreducible kinds of thing
meaning: Dualism, in the philosophy of mind, is the view that the mind and the body, the mental and the physical, are in some fundamental sense distinct and irreducible kinds of thing, so that mental phenomena are not simply physical. It stands opposed to physicalism, the view that everything, including the mind, is ultimately physical. Dualism comes in two main forms. Substance dualism, also called Cartesian dualism after René Descartes, holds that mind and body are two fundamentally different kinds of substance: the mind an immaterial, thinking substance and the body a physical, extended substance. Property dualism, the more common contemporary form, holds that there is only one kind of substance, the physical, but that it possesses two essentially different kinds of property, physical properties and non-physical mental properties, such as qualia or conscious experiences, that are not reducible to the physical. Dualists appeal to arguments such as the apparent irreducibility of consciousness, the knowledge argument, and the conceivability of philosophical zombies to argue that the mental cannot be wholly physical. The chief objection to dualism, especially substance dualism, is the interaction problem: how a non-physical mind could causally interact with a physical body. Historically dominant, dualism remains a serious minority position in contemporary philosophy of mind.
mechanism: Dualism answers the mind-body problem by denying that the mental can be reduced to or identified with the physical. In its substance form, associated with Descartes, the claim is that a human being consists of two distinct substances: a mind whose essence is thought and which is non-extended and indivisible, and a body whose essence is spatial extension and which is divisible and governed by physics. The mind and body are really distinct, capable in principle of existing apart, yet in life they interact, the mind directing the body and the body affecting the mind. In its property form, the more common view today, dualism accepts that there is only physical substance but insists that some of its properties, specifically the phenomenal properties of conscious experience, are not physical properties and cannot be reduced to or fully explained by them. Dualists support these claims with several arguments: the knowledge argument, that a person who knew every physical fact about color could still learn something new on seeing red, suggesting non-physical facts; the conceivability of a philosophical zombie, a physical duplicate of a person that lacks consciousness, suggesting consciousness is over and above the physical; and the apparent explanatory gap between physical descriptions and subjective experience. The great difficulty for dualism is mental causation: if the mind is non-physical, how does it cause physical events, given the apparent causal closure of the physical world, in which every physical effect already has a sufficient physical cause.

examples.text: Descartes held mind and body are two distinct substances, an immaterial thinking mind and a physical extended body.
Property dualism holds there is one physical substance but with irreducible non-physical mental properties, such as qualia.
The main objection asks how a non-physical mind could causally interact with a physical body.

whyItMatters: Dualism is one of the most important and historically dominant positions in the philosophy of mind, giving philosophical form to the deep intuition that the conscious mind is something more than mere physical matter. By holding that the mental and the physical are fundamentally distinct, dualism frames the central debate of the field against physicalism and keeps alive the question of whether consciousness can be fully explained in physical terms. Descartes's substance dualism set the terms of the modern mind-body problem, and its difficulties, above all the interaction problem, have shaped centuries of philosophical work. In its contemporary property-dualist form, defended by philosophers such as David Chalmers, dualism draws on powerful arguments about consciousness, the knowledge argument, philosophical zombies, and the explanatory gap, to challenge the prevailing physicalist consensus and to insist that subjective experience resists reduction. Dualism thus remains a live and influential option, taken seriously by a substantial minority of philosophers, and it bears on debates about the soul, personal identity, free will, and whether machines could be conscious. As the view that mind and matter are distinct in kind, dualism is central to how we think about the nature of mind.

limits: Dualism faces serious and well-known objections that keep it a minority view. The central problem, especially for substance dualism, is the interaction problem, or the problem of mental causation: it is hard to explain how a non-physical mind could causally affect a physical body, particularly given the apparent causal closure of the physical world, in which every physical effect already has a sufficient physical cause, which threatens to make the mental causally idle or to violate conservation laws. Dualism also sits uneasily with the success and parsimony of physical science, and considerations of simplicity are often taken to favor physicalism. Property dualism avoids positing a separate substance but still must explain how irreducible mental properties fit into a physical world and do any causal work. Surveys of philosophers show dualism as a substantial minority, roughly a fifth, against a physicalist majority. So dualism robustly expresses the distinctness of the mental from the physical, understood as a historically dominant but now minority position burdened by the interaction problem and its tension with physical science.
misreadings: Dualism is not a single view; substance dualism posits two distinct substances, while property dualism posits one substance with irreducible mental properties, and the two differ importantly. It is not obviously true just because consciousness feels non-physical, since it must answer the interaction problem and its tension with physical science, which is why it is a minority view. And it is not refuted merely by the success of neuroscience, since the arguments about consciousness remain, so treating dualism as one uniform view, as self-evidently correct, or as simply disproven by science, misreads a serious but contested position on the mind.
origin: The view in philosophy of mind, associated above all with René Descartes, that mind and body are fundamentally distinct and irreducible kinds of thing, whether distinct substances or distinct properties; opposed to physicalism.
